primary_focus: Solidify your ability to generalize the one-pass hash-map complement pattern to variants (multiple answers, returning all pairs, sorted input) while keeping index correctness and complexity guarantees explicit.
thinking_and_logic: You correctly identified brute force as O(n^2) and chose the canonical optimization: maintain a hash map from value to index while iterating, and for each number check whether its complement has already been seen. Checking the complement before inserting the current number prevents using the same element twice and naturally supports duplicate values by storing earlier indices and matching when the second instance appears.
code_assessment: Your final code matches the answer key’s optimal solution (single pass + hash map). Compared to the brute-force approach, it achieves O(n) time by converting the inner-loop search into O(1) average-time lookups, at the cost of O(n) extra space. It also avoids the common pitfalls in the answer key: it doesn’t sort (so indices stay correct), it doesn’t reuse an element (complement check before insert), and it handles duplicates correctly.

transcript.text: Here's the problem: given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target. Take your time to read it.
Okay. Quick clarification — is there always exactly one valid answer, and can I use the same element twice?
Exactly one valid answer exists, and you may not use the same element twice.

Got it. The brute force is checking every pair, which is O(n squared). But I can do better with a hash map: as I scan, I store each value with its index, and for each element I check whether target minus the current value is already in the map. That's a single pass, O(n) time, O(n) space. I'll go with that.
Writing it now. I'm checking the complement before inserting the current value so I never match an element with itself. That also handles duplicates like two threes summing to six.
Done. Let me trace it with nums = [2, 7, 11, 15], target 9: i=0 stores 2, i=1 complement is 2 which is in the map, so I return [0, 1]. I'll run the tests.
All visible tests pass. Can you state the complexity of your solution?
Time is O(n) — one pass, each lookup and insert is amortized O(1). Space is O(n) for the map in the worst case.
Follow-up: what would you change if the input array were sorted?
Then I'd use two pointers from both ends and move them inward based on whether the sum is too big or too small. That keeps O(n) time but drops the extra space to O(1).
Great. That wraps up the interview.
